how-to-pin-a-docker-base-image-to-a-dige.text:
← Docker Base Image Pin Check

How to pin a Docker base image to a digest

Short answer: the Digest: line from docker buildx imagetools inspect is the value to use — replace the tag with @<that digest>, keeping the original tag as a trailing comment so a human reading the Dockerfile still knows which version it is.

Most Dockerfiles start like this:

FROM node:18

18 is a tag, and a tag is just a name someone attached to an image build — the publisher can push a new build to that same tag at any time. Pinning to a content digest instead means the reference cannot be silently changed: a digest addresses one exact set of bytes.

1. Find the digest a tag currently resolves to

Use docker buildx imagetools inspect against the image and tag. This queries the registry's manifest directly — the same request a docker pull would make to decide what to fetch — without pulling the full image:

docker buildx imagetools inspect node:18

That prints output including a line like:

Name:      docker.io/library/node:18
MediaType: application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json
Digest:    sha256:7e2895622100fa27781b8d926d4c7d719f26061ba1e78facbf3f6352a6407965

The Digest: line is the value to use. (No buildx available? docker manifest inspect --verbose node:18 or the third-party crane digest node:18 answer the same question.)

2. Replace the tag with the digest

Keep the original tag as a trailing comment, so a human reading the Dockerfile still knows which version it is without decoding the hash:

FROM node@sha256:7e2895622100fa27781b8d926d4c7d719f26061ba1e78facbf3f6352a6407965 # 18

That line now resolves to exactly one set of bytes, forever. Upgrading later is a deliberate, reviewable diff: look up the digest for a newer tag and replace both the hash and the comment.

3. Do this for every FROM line, in every Dockerfile

A multi-stage build can have several FROM lines, and a single unpinned reference is enough to be the weak link — including the final stage that actually ships. Paste your Dockerfile into Docker Base Image Pin Check to find every mutable reference at once, each with its own ready-to-run imagetools inspect command, or run the CLI in your own repository:

python3 check.py --fail-on-risk

That exits with a nonzero status if any base image is still referenced by a tag instead of a digest — wire it into your own CI to block a newly-added unpinned base image before it merges.

Why a version-looking tag is not enough

node:18 is a moving target for the entire support lifetime of Node 18: the maintainers push new patch and security builds to that same tag routinely, which is the point of the tag — you want those updates when you rebuild deliberately. The risk this addresses is the same update landing silently, on someone else's docker build, with nothing in your own commit history to say the base image changed. A digest reference removes that ambiguity: the same digest always means the same bytes, so a change of base image is a change you make on purpose, in a diff you can review.

No warranty. This page and the tool it describes are provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind. Confirm any digest yourself before pinning to it, and verify before relying on the output. This is not a security audit or a compliance attestation, and it does not tell you whether the code inside that image is itself safe to run — only which content digest a tag currently resolves to.

index.html.text:
DOCKER BASE IMAGE PIN CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Are your Dockerfile base images pinned to a digest?

A base image referenced by a tag (node:18) or nothing at all (node, which resolves to :latest) trusts whatever bytes that tag points to right now — and its publisher can push a new build to that same tag tomorrow, silently, with no version bump to review. Paste your Dockerfile below and this page finds every FROM line that isn't pinned to a content digest, with the exact command to look up the digest yourself.

Nothing is uploaded. The Dockerfile you paste is read in this browser and never leaves your device, and this tool makes no network calls of its own — not even to look up the digest for you.

1. Paste one or more Dockerfiles

Copy the contents of each Dockerfile (or Dockerfile.* / *.dockerfile) you want checked. Add more blocks for more files — nothing here reads your repository, so pasting is how it sees anything.

Paste at least one Dockerfile above and click Check.

Findings

File : LineImageTag / DigestStatusFix

Prefer a CLI, or want this in your own CI?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file:

python3 check.py                  # scan every Dockerfile under the current directory
python3 check.py /path/to/repo    # scan a specific checkout
python3 check.py --format json    # machine-readable
python3 check.py --fail-on-risk   # exit 2 if any mutable (unpinned) base image is found

Get check.py from the repo — stdlib only, nothing to install, no network calls. Wire --fail-on-risk into your own CI to block a newly-added unpinned base image before it merges.

Common questions

Why is a tag like node:18 a risk if it looks like a specific version?

A tag — even a specific-looking one like :18 — is a name someone attached to an image, and the publisher can push a new build to that same tag at any time. The next time you run docker build, you pull whatever bytes that tag now points to, with no version bump to review and no diff to notice. A content digest (@sha256:...) addresses one exact set of bytes and cannot be silently repointed, which is why Docker's own base-image guidance and the SLSA framework's build-provenance requirements both recommend pinning to it.

Does this tool fetch or pull anything for me?

No. It makes no network calls at all — nothing here can, because nothing here talks to a registry. For every mutable reference it finds, it prints the exact docker buildx imagetools inspect command you can run yourself to look up the digest that tag currently resolves to. The lookup, and the decision to pin, stay entirely yours.

Does a clean scan mean my build is supply-chain safe?

No. This checks one specific, well-documented thing: whether a FROM line references its base image by content digest. It is not a security audit, and it makes no claim about your build's overall supply-chain security or the safety of the code inside a pinned image.

What about multi-stage builds and FROM scratch?

A FROM line that names an earlier build stage (FROM builder, after a prior FROM ... AS builder) is not a registry pull and is skipped, as is FROM scratch, Docker's empty virtual base image that cannot be repointed. A FROM line containing a build-arg substitution like ${BASE_IMAGE} is also skipped, since the actual image cannot be determined from the Dockerfile text alone — resolve the build argument's value and re-run.

More: how to pin a Docker base image to a digest. Already run Hadolint? See how this checker compares for the pinning question specifically. Prefer to just read the file? See this checker vs. reading a Dockerfile by hand.

Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Digest-pinning a base image doesn't catch every container supply-chain risk: Pinned Actions Check asks the same "mutable tag vs. immutable reference" question for the GitHub Actions uses: lines that build and push that image, and npm Lifecycle Script Check flags install-time scripts in the dependency tree the image's own RUN npm install pulls in — two more slices of a hardened build pipeline. Docker Build Secrets Check asks a third question of the same Dockerfile: whether an ENV, ARG, or copied file bakes a credential into the image this tool never looks for, and Docker Cache Order Check asks a fourth: whether the same Dockerfile's instruction order busts the build cache. And pinning is not the same as supported: a reference can be pinned to an exact digest and still be built from a release line nobody patches anymore — Docker Base Image EOL Check asks that question of the same FROM line. Once the image is pinned and built, Kubernetes Rollout Safety Check asks the next question down the same pipeline: whether deploying it drops live requests. Already generate an SBOM for that image? SBOM Diff Check shows exactly which packages changed between two builds.

Free and open source. If this saved you from shipping a mutable base image, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-hadolint.html.text:
← Docker Base Image Pin Check

Docker Base Image Pin Check vs. Hadolint

Related tools, different jobs. Hadolint is a broad Dockerfile linter whose own tagging rules stop at "has an explicit, non-latest tag" -- so node:18 passes it clean. This page checks the next question directly: is that tag a content digest, free, in your browser, with no install.

What each tool is for

Hadolint (github.com/hadolint/hadolint) is an open-source Dockerfile linter covering dozens of rules -- its own DL-prefixed rule set plus ShellCheck applied to every RUN instruction -- across style, correctness, and best practices for an entire Dockerfile. It runs as a CLI, a Docker image, or a pre-commit hook, typically wired into CI. Two of its rules touch base-image tagging: by its own rule documentation, DL3006 ("Always tag the version of an image explicitly") flags a FROM line with no tag at all, and DL3007 ("Using latest is prone to errors if the image will ever update. Pin the version explicitly to a release tag") flags an explicit :latest tag. Neither rule requires a digest.

This checker does one narrower thing: you paste the text of a Dockerfile, and it lists every FROM line whose base image is not pinned to a content digest -- file, line, the mutable reference it found, and the exact docker buildx imagetools inspect command to look up the digest yourself. A line like FROM node:18 satisfies both of Hadolint's tagging rules and passes clean, while still being a mutable reference this tool flags: the publisher can push a new build to the 18 tag at any time, with nothing in the Dockerfile changing to show it. It runs entirely in your browser, needs no install, and makes no network call of its own.

Where to answer each question.
QuestionWhere to answer it
Does my Dockerfile have shell-scripting mistakes in a RUN instruction, unnecessary layers, or other style/correctness issues across the whole file?Hadolint -- that is its entire job, and this tool does not attempt any of it.
Which exact FROM lines reference a base image by tag instead of digest, and what do I run to fix each one?This checker -- a file:line list with a copy-pasteable remediation command, not a rule-violation count.
My FROM line has an explicit, specific version tag like :18 -- is that enough?No, and only this checker says so directly: DL3006/DL3007 are both satisfied by an explicit non-latest tag, so Hadolint reports it clean.
I want this wired into CI to block a merge automatically.Either: Hadolint's own CI integration for its broad rule set, or this tool's check.py --fail-on-risk for the digest-pinning question specifically.

The two are complementary, not competing: a repository can run Hadolint for the broad linting pass it is built for and still reach for this tool for the one question Hadolint's own tagging rules stop short of.

Run the free base image pin check

Common questions

Should I use this checker or Hadolint?

They are different shapes of tool for a related but different question. Hadolint is a broad Dockerfile linter -- dozens of rules (its own DL-prefixed rule set plus ShellCheck applied to every RUN instruction) covering style, correctness, and best practices across an entire Dockerfile, run as a CLI, a Docker image, or a pre-commit hook. This tool checks exactly one thing: whether each FROM line's base image is pinned to a content digest, and instead of a rule-violation count it lists every unpinned reference individually with the exact docker buildx imagetools inspect command to look up the digest. If you want broad Dockerfile linting -- shell-scripting mistakes in RUN, missing WORKDIR, unnecessary layers, and more -- Hadolint is the right tool and this one does not attempt any of that. If you want the specific answer to "which FROM lines are not digest-pinned, and what do I run to fix each one," this is the narrower tool for that question.

Doesn't Hadolint already flag an unpinned base image?

Partially, and this is the exact gap this tool exists to close. Hadolint's own rule documentation describes DL3006 ("Always tag the version of an image explicitly") as flagging a FROM line with no tag at all, and DL3007 ("Using latest is prone to errors if the image will ever update. Pin the version explicitly to a release tag") as flagging an explicit :latest tag. Neither rule requires a digest. A line like FROM node:18 satisfies both -- it has an explicit, non-latest tag -- and passes Hadolint clean by design, while still being a mutable reference: the publisher can push a new build to the 18 tag at any time, with nothing in your Dockerfile changing. This tool flags exactly that case, which Hadolint's own documented rules do not cover.

Why would I need a separate checker if Hadolint already exists?

Two reasons. First, the coverage gap above: Hadolint's tagging rules stop at "has an explicit, non-latest tag," and this tool's entire reason to exist is the next step, "is that tag a content digest." Second, Hadolint is a Haskell binary (or a Docker image) you install and run; this tool is also available as a page you open with nothing to install, for a quick check on a Dockerfile you have not wired into a linter yet. Neither point is a criticism of Hadolint's own scope -- its rule set is deliberately broad and well beyond base-image pinning, which is exactly why a narrower, purpose-built check for this one question is worth having alongside it.

Is this page affiliated with Hadolint?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by the Hadolint project or its maintainers. Hadolint is an open-source Dockerfile linter, named here only to describe what this checker is and is not, using facts drawn from Hadolint's own public rule documentation and source repository at github.com/hadolint/hadolint.

vs-reading-a-dockerfile-by-hand.html.text:
← Back to Docker Base Image Pin Check

Docker Base Image Pin Check vs. reading a Dockerfile by hand

Skimming a Dockerfile for an obvious FROM node or FROM node:latest genuinely works, and it is the method most people already use. This page names no product or company being compared against: "reading the Dockerfile by hand" is a generic manual habit, not a competing tool.

CaseReading the Dockerfile by handThis tool
Bare FROM node or explicit FROM node:latestCorrectly caught by a reviewer who knows to look for itCorrectly caught the same way
A specific-looking tag, FROM node:18Reads as already careful -- easy to not flag, even though the tag can still be repointedClassifies any non-digest tag as mutable, specific-looking or not
A later FROM builder referencing an earlier AS builder stageRequires remembering every stage alias defined earlier in a long file to avoid a false alarmTracks every AS <name> alias while scanning and checks later FROM lines against that running set automatically
A private registry reference with a port, myregistry.local:5000/node:18Easy to misread the port's colon as the tag delimiterAlways locates the tag inside the last /-separated path segment, never the host
Multiple Dockerfiles across a repository (Dockerfile, Dockerfile.prod, worker.dockerfile)Coverage depends on remembering every file existsCLI discovers every matching filename under a directory on its own

The gap that matters most: the specific-looking tag

node:18 is the trap this tool exists to catch. It reads as more careful than bare node or node:latest, and it is not pinned in the sense that matters -- Docker still resolves 18 to whatever bytes that tag points to right now, and unlike a version bump you would review, a later push to the same tag is silent. A reviewer scanning for "obviously risky" names has no reason to single this out. This tool draws no such distinction: anything short of a content digest classifies as mutable, regardless of how specific the tag looks.

The gap that matters second: telling a build stage from a registry pull

A multi-stage Dockerfile reuses names for its own internal stages, and a later FROM <name> that refers to one of them is not a registry pull at all -- it has no tag to pin. Getting this right by eye means holding every AS <name> alias defined earlier in the file in mind while reading each subsequent FROM line, which gets harder as a Dockerfile grows more stages. This tool tracks the alias set mechanically as it scans, so the distinction does not depend on what a reader remembered from forty lines up.

When to still read the Dockerfile yourself

This tool answers one question -- is this FROM line pinned to a content digest -- and stops there. It does not resolve a mutable tag to a digest for you (it prints the docker buildx imagetools inspect command instead), and it makes no claim about whether the code inside a pinned image is itself safe. Deciding whether to trust a given digest, and reviewing what a base image actually contains, is still a job for you.

Common questions

What does reading a Dockerfile by hand actually catch?

A reviewer who knows to look for it can spot the obvious case immediately: FROM node with no tag at all, or an explicit FROM node:latest. Both read as risky on sight, because latest is a well-known name for "whatever the publisher pushed most recently." That review genuinely works for the obvious case -- the same case this tool's classify.mjs also flags.

Why does a specific-looking tag like node:18 slip past a skim?

node:18 reads as more careful than bare node or node:latest, because it names a specific major version -- but Docker still resolves :18 to whatever bytes that tag currently points to, and the publisher can push a new build to it at any time with no version bump to review. A reviewer scanning for the word "latest" or a missing tag has no reason to flag node:18, since nothing about it looks wrong. This tool draws no such distinction: every tag, specific-looking or not, that isn't a content digest classifies as mutable.

Why is telling a build-stage reference apart from a registry pull easy to get wrong by eye?

A multi-stage Dockerfile can define FROM golang:1.22 AS builder early on and then write FROM builder forty lines later to continue that stage -- and FROM builder is not a registry pull at all, so it has no tag to pin and nothing to flag. A reviewer working through a long Dockerfile has to remember every stage alias defined earlier in the file to make that call correctly; forgetting one risks either a false alarm on a name that is not a registry image, or missing that a later re-use of the same word is a genuine external FROM. This tool tracks every AS <name> alias as it scans and checks each later FROM against that running set automatically, so the distinction never depends on what a reader kept in their head.

Why is a registry with a port number easy to misread?

A reference like myregistry.local:5000/node:18 contains two colons, and naively splitting on the first one reads :5000/node as the tag -- nonsense that hides the real tag, 18. The actual grammar is that a colon only starts a tag inside the last slash-separated path segment; the colon in registry:5000/ is part of the host, not a tag delimiter. Getting this right by eye on an unfamiliar private-registry reference is easy to get backwards. This tool's splitNameAndRef always locates the tag inside the last path segment only, so a registry port is never misread as one.

Does this replace checking every Dockerfile in a repository?

No, but it removes the tedium of doing so by hand. A repository can carry a Dockerfile, a Dockerfile.prod, and a worker.dockerfile, each with its own FROM lines, and a manual review has to remember to open every one, every time a new file is added. The CLI (python3 check.py) discovers Dockerfile, Dockerfile.*, and *.dockerfile anywhere under a given directory on its own, so coverage does not depend on a reviewer's memory of which files exist.

Evidence, not a determination. This checks one specific, well-documented thing -- whether a FROM line is pinned to a content digest. A clean report describes what that check found, not a guarantee your build is safe from supply-chain attacks generally.
